# Introduction

This project explores quantitative and qualitative fruit characteristics across three simulated guava accessions. The analysis demonstrates a practical workflow for data preparation, exploratory data analysis, visualization, and statistical testing using R.

The project is inspired by an agricultural research workflow involving fruit characterization and accession comparison. However, all observations used in this project are simulated and do not represent actual experimental records.

# Objectives

The objectives are to:

- Validate the dataset and calculate a derived fruit shape index.
- Summarize fruit characteristics and compare descriptive statistics across accessions.
- Explore relationships between numerical variables.
- Evaluate whether mean Brix values differ across accessions using appropriate statistical tests.

# Dataset Description

The dataset contains 75 simulated fruit observations distributed equally across three accessions: A01, A02, and A03, with 25 observations per accession.

Variables include fruit weight, length, width, peel color, Brix, firmness, and seed count. A fruit shape index is calculated as fruit length divided by fruit width.

The data are intended for demonstration and learning purposes. Findings should not be interpreted as conclusions about real guava accessions or as evidence of genetic differences.

# Data Preparation and Validation

```{r setup-data, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# Load the simulated guava dataset
guava_data <- read.csv(file.choose())

# Calculate data quality indicators
total_observations <- nrow(guava_data)
total_variables <- ncol(guava_data)
missing_values <- sum(is.na(guava_data))
duplicate_rows <- sum(duplicated(guava_data))
duplicate_ids <- sum(duplicated(guava_data$fruit_id))
```

This project uses a simulated dataset of guava fruit measurements across three accessions. The dataset was prepared for portfolio demonstration and does not contain original research records.

Data quality checks were performed to assess dataset completeness and consistency before conducting the statistical analysis.

```{r data-quality, echo=FALSE}
data.frame(
  Metric = c(
    "Observations",
    "Variables",
    "Missing values",
    "Duplicate rows",
    "Duplicate fruit IDs"
  ),
  Result = c(
    total_observations,
    total_variables,
    missing_values,
    duplicate_rows,
    duplicate_ids
  )
)
```

# Exploratory Data Analysis

An additional quantitative variable, the fruit shape index, was calculated as fruit length divided by fruit width. This derived measure was included to explore fruit proportions and relationships among numerical traits.

```{r, include=FALSE}
# Calculate fruit shape index
guava_data$fruit_shape_index <-
  guava_data$fruit_length_cm / guava_data$fruit_width_cm
```

## Descriptive Statistics

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Select key quantitative variables
descriptive_data <- guava_data[, c(
  "fruit_weight_g",
  "fruit_length_cm",
  "fruit_width_cm",
  "brix",
  "firmness_kgf_cm2",
  "seed_count",
  "fruit_shape_index"
)]

# Generate descriptive statistics
descriptive_stats <- data.frame(
  Variable = names(descriptive_data),
row.names = NULL,
  Mean = sapply(descriptive_data, mean, na.rm = TRUE),
  Median = sapply(descriptive_data, median, na.rm = TRUE),
  SD = sapply(descriptive_data, sd, na.rm = TRUE),
  Minimum = sapply(descriptive_data, min, na.rm = TRUE),
  Maximum = sapply(descriptive_data, max, na.rm = TRUE)
)

# Round numerical results
descriptive_stats[, -1] <- round(descriptive_stats[, -1], 2)

rownames(descriptive_stats) <- NULL

knitr::kable(
  descriptive_stats,
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Descriptive Statistics of Guava Fruit Traits"
)
```

## Comparison of Accession Means

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Calculate mean values for each accession
accession_means <- aggregate(
  cbind(
    fruit_weight_g,
    fruit_length_cm,
    fruit_width_cm,
    brix
  ) ~ accession,
  data = guava_data,
  FUN = mean
)

# Round numerical results
accession_means[, -1] <- round(accession_means[, -1], 2)

# Display formatted table
knitr::kable(
  accession_means,
  digits = 2,
  col.names = c(
    "Accession",
    "Mean Weight (g)",
    "Mean Length (cm)",
    "Mean Width (cm)",
    "Mean Brix (°Bx)"
  ),
  caption = "Mean Fruit Characteristics by Accession",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

## Brix Distribution

```{r, fig.width=6, fig.height=3.5}
# Compare Brix values across accessions
boxplot(
  brix ~ accession,
  data = guava_data,
  main = "Brix Distribution Across Guava Accessions",
  xlab = "Accession",
  ylab = "Brix (°Bx)",
 col = c("#4393C3", "#FDDBC7", "#D6604D"),
border = c("#2166AC", "#E8B99F", "#B2182B"),
  medcol = "#333333",
  whiskcol = "#555555",
  staplecol = "#555555",
  outcol = "#555555",
  outpch = 16,
  frame.plot = FALSE
)
```

# Statistical Analysis

## Classical One-Way ANOVA

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Compare mean Brix across accessions using classical ANOVA
brix_anova <- aov(brix ~ accession, data = guava_data)

summary(brix_anova)
```

## ANOVA Assumption Checks

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6.5, fig.height=4.5}
# Check normality of ANOVA residuals
shapiro.test(residuals(brix_anova))

# Display diagnostic plots
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(brix_anova, col.lines = "#E9A15B")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Check homogeneity of variances
bartlett.test(brix ~ accession, data = guava_data)
```

The Shapiro-Wilk test did not provide evidence against the normality of the ANOVA residuals (p = 0.5429). However, Bartlett’s test indicated unequal variances across accessions (p = 0.0237). Therefore, Welch’s ANOVA was selected as the primary overall comparison.

## Welch's ANOVA

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Compare mean Brix across accessions without assuming equal variances
welch_anova <- oneway.test(
  brix ~ accession,
  data = guava_data,
  var.equal = FALSE
)

welch_anova
```

## Post-hoc Comparisons

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Perform Tukey HSD pairwise comparisons
tukey_results <- TukeyHSD(brix_anova)

# Convert results into a data frame
tukey_table <- as.data.frame(tukey_results$accession)

# Add comparison names as a column
tukey_table$Comparison <- rownames(tukey_table)

# Reorder columns
tukey_table <- tukey_table[, c(
  "Comparison",
  "diff",
  "lwr",
  "upr",
  "p adj"
)]

# Display formatted results
knitr::kable(
  tukey_table,
  digits = 3,
  col.names = c(
    "Comparison",
    "Mean Difference",
    "CI Lower",
    "CI Upper",
    "Adjusted p-value"
  ),
  caption = "Tukey HSD Pairwise Comparisons",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

Tukey HSD is presented as a reference comparison under the equal-variance assumption. Given the evidence of unequal variances, Games–Howell is considered more appropriate for pairwise comparisons.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Perform Games-Howell pairwise comparisons
games_howell_results <- rstatix::games_howell_test(
  guava_data,
  brix ~ accession
)

# Select relevant columns for reporting
games_howell_table <- games_howell_results[, c(
  "group1",
  "group2",
  "estimate",
  "conf.low",
  "conf.high",
  "p.adj",
  "p.adj.signif"
)]

# Display formatted results
knitr::kable(
  games_howell_table,
  digits = 3,
  col.names = c(
    "Group 1",
    "Group 2",
    "Mean Difference",
    "CI Lower",
    "CI Upper",
    "Adjusted p-value",
    "Significance"
  ),
  caption = "Games-Howell Pairwise Comparisons",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

# Correlation Analysis

```{r, include=FALSE, fig.width=6, fig.height=3.5}
# Select numeric variables for correlation analysis
numeric_data <- guava_data[, c(
  "fruit_weight_g",
  "fruit_length_cm",
  "fruit_width_cm",
  "brix",
  "firmness_kgf_cm2",
  "seed_count",
  "fruit_shape_index"
)]
```


```{r, fig.width=9, fig.height=8}

# Calculate the correlation matrix
correlation_matrix <- cor(
  numeric_data,
  use = "complete.obs"
)

# Create shorter labels for the plot
short_labels <- c(
  "Weight",
  "Length",
  "Width",
  "Brix",
  "Firmness",
  "Seeds",
  "Shape"
)

# Apply short labels to the correlation matrix
dimnames(correlation_matrix) <- list(
  short_labels,
  short_labels
)

# Visualize the correlations
corrplot::corrplot(
  correlation_matrix,
  method = "color",
  type = "upper",
  addCoef.col = "black",
  tl.col = "black",
  tl.srt = 0,
  tl.cex = 1.2,
  cl.cex = 1.1,
  number.cex = 1.1,
  diag = FALSE,
  mar = c(0, 0, 2, 0)
)
```

# Conclusions and Recommendations

## Key Findings

The descriptive analysis revealed differences in fruit characteristics across the three simulated guava accessions. A01 had the highest average fruit weight (180.45 g), while A02 showed the highest average Brix value (11.92 °Bx). These results illustrate that accessions can differ across traits, and that no single accession necessarily performs best across every characteristic.

The correlation analysis identified moderate positive relationships between fruit weight and both fruit length (r = 0.582) and fruit width (r = 0.597). A moderate negative relationship was observed between fruit weight and Brix (r = -0.340). These patterns describe associations within the simulated dataset and should not be interpreted as evidence of causation.

## Statistical Assessment

The initial classical ANOVA suggested a potential difference in mean Brix values. However, Bartlett’s test provided evidence of unequal group variances (p = 0.0237).

Given the evidence of unequal variances, the Games–Howell procedure was used for pairwise comparisons because it does not assume equal group variances.

Therefore, Welch’s ANOVA was used as the more appropriate overall comparison. Its result was not statistically significant at the 0.05 level (p = 0.0968). Games–Howell pairwise comparisons also found no statistically significant differences between accessions.

Consequently, the analysis does not provide sufficient statistical evidence to conclude that mean Brix differs across the three accessions. This does not prove that the accessions are identical; further evaluation with additional data may be warranted.

## Recommendations and Limitations

For a real agricultural research study, the next step would be to collect additional observations under controlled and documented conditions and validate whether the observed patterns persist. Accession selection should consider multiple traits and research objectives rather than relying on a single measurement.

This project uses simulated data created for analytical demonstration. Its findings are intended to illustrate data validation, exploratory analysis, correlation assessment, and statistical testing in R. They do not represent experimentally confirmed differences among real guava accessions.
